title: Chicago, 1893
hookLine: at the World's Parliament of Religions, Dharmapala and the Zen teacher Soyen Shaku speak
last: A DEWDROP SLIPPING INTO THE SHINING SEA.

cards: A big hall in Chicago, a long row of speakers on the stage. People of many faiths have been invited to stand up, one after another, and explain their own tradition to a crowd of strangers.

Some in the seats have read about the Buddha in books like yesterday's poem. Now a Buddhist stands in front of them: a young man from Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, in a plain white robe, Anagarika Dharmapala.
Beside him on the program, a Zen abbot from Japan named Soyen Shaku.

teach.b: It was called the World's Parliament of Religions, and it met alongside a great fair in Chicago.
Its organizers wanted the religions of the world side by side, each in its own words, and they printed the speeches afterward, so we can still read them.
Dharmapala had spent his young life working to restore Buddhist places in India, above all Bodh Gaya, where the Buddha woke up under the tree.
In Chicago he spoke of the Buddha as a teacher of reason and kindness, whose way was open to anyone willing to practice it.
Soyen Shaku was the abbot of a Zen temple in Kamakura, and he did not speak English. His talk, on cause and effect, was put into English and read to the hall for him.
Accounts say a young lay student of his helped with the English: D. T. Suzuki, who comes back tomorrow.
Why it matters: some in that hall had met the Buddha only in books by outsiders. Here, Buddhists spoke for themselves.

The Dhammapada has a line that fits a week of long speeches: "Even though a speech be a thousand (of words), but made up of senseless words, one word of sense is better, which if a man hears, he becomes quiet."
In a hall full of speeches, that was the hope.

how: Buddhists in Sri Lanka honor Anagarika Dharmapala as a reviver of the teaching and of the sites in India, and Japanese Zen remembers Soyen Shaku as a teacher who brought Zen before Western listeners.

games.q: you're a Zen abbot invited to speak to a hall of strangers in a country whose language you don't speak. what do you do?
o: stay home and send a letter of regret.

games.why: Soyen Shaku's talk on cause and effect was put into English and read for him, and accounts say his young student D. T. Suzuki helped.

practice: Say one true sentence about your own practice, out loud or quietly, maybe: I sit for a couple of minutes most days, or, I'm still working out what my practice is. Say it once, slowly.
Then stop, close your eyes, and sit in the quiet after it, the way one word of sense leaves the hearer quiet.

wordCard.voice: Chicago. Where, at a parliament of faiths, Dharmapala and Soyen Shaku stood up and spoke for the Buddha's teaching in their own voices.

orig.note: Pali dhamma (Sanskrit dharma): the teaching that Dharmapala and Soyen Shaku stood up to speak for.

carryVoice: Your line: the teaching speaks. One word of sense outweighs a thousand. See you tomorrow.
